setting: A short lecture in a public health class about antibiotics and why resistance is a growing problem.
narrator_intro: Listen to part of a talk in a public health class.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria or stop them from growing.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: They transformed medicine by making once-deadly infections treatable.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: But bacteria can evolve defenses, a process we call antibiotic resistance.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: When antibiotics are used too often or stopped too early, resistant strains are more likely to survive.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Those resistant bacteria can spread between people in hospitals, communities, and even through food systems.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Doctors now face infections that need stronger drugs—or combinations—because first-line antibiotics fail.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Public health advice stresses using antibiotics only when needed and finishing the prescribed course.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Researchers also look for new drugs and better tests that identify the right treatment faster.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: In short, antibiotics remain powerful tools, but misuse threatens their future effectiveness.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Next week we’ll review case studies of hospital infection-control programs.

narrator_outro: Now get ready to answer the questions.
